..(After midnight Friday night through Wednesday)
Issued at 618 AM EST Thu Nov 12 2026

The forecast guidance suite continues to collectively resolve broad 
longwave troughing over the Eastern CONUS this weekend, with Eastern 
Kentucky situated upon its southwestern periphery from Friday night 
through Sunday morning. The persistence of this pattern corresponds 
with a prolonged period of deep northwesterly flow over the forecast 
area, and the resultant cold air advection regime should culminate 
in the coldest high and low temperature readings of the season thus 
far. Such a setup also favors enhanced low-level moisture (via a 
fetch off the Great Lakes) and enhanced orographic lift along the 
area's NW facing slopes. Those enhancements should combine with the 
approach of an embedded shortwave impulse aloft to yield continued 
precipitation chances on Friday night/Saturday morning, and it is 
plausible for portions of the forecast area to see their first 
flakes of the season in this time frame.   

While it looks sufficiently cold enough for snow in the mountains of 
SE KY during the short term forecast period on Friday afternoon, 
surface temperatures probably won't be cold enough for snow 
elsewhere until the long term period starts on Friday night. The 
latest high resolution ensemble guidance resolves a greater than 55% 
chance for temperatures to approach the freezing point across all 
but our northeastern-most counties on Saturday morning, which 
suggests that any ongoing rain showers will be able to mix with or 
transition over to snow. Antecedent soil temperatures are too warm 
for this activity to yield meaningful accumulations, but a dusting 
cannot be ruled out on elevated surfaces in places along/southeast 
of the Pottsville Escarpment. Said accumulations are most likely if 
cloud cover and precipitation chances linger in these upsloped 
places into the afternoon hours on Saturday, which is a plausible 
scenario. 

Pattern recognition and past forecaster experience suggest that the 
baseline NBM guidance typically clears skies and tapers PoPs off too 
quickly in this kind of northwesterly flow setup. Persistent upslope 
flow and moist low-level sounding profiles suggest that Saturday's 
clouds could be quite stubborn downwind of the escarpment. As 
such, have held on to PoPs and bolstered sky grids in the opening 
stages of the forecast period. The greater cloud cover should mute
the diurnal heating curve and relegate afternoon highs to the 
lower half of the 40s in most places. Some forecast guidance even 
keeps the mountains of SE KY in the upper 30s on Saturday 
afternoon, which makes sense given that these locations are also 
the most likely to see accumulating snow. Clouds should 
theoretically hold on the longest there, which introduces some 
uncertainty into Saturday night's low temperature forecast. On the
other hand, areas west of I- 75 are the most likely to clear out 
and the least likely to see continued snow showers/flurries. Even 
there, highs are unlikely to reach the 50 degree mark, making 
Saturday the coolest day of the season thus far.

The coldest night(s) of the season will come later in the period 
though, as the troughing is progged to gradually propagate away from 
the forecast area early next week. An amplified upstream ridge and 
its corresponding surface high pressure system will begin to exert 
their influence on the Ohio River Valley on Sunday. This should 
shift winds towards a more northerly/northeasterly orientation and 
facilitate a clearing trend. While modeled midlevel height rises and 
mostly sunny skies should accordingly allow highs to moderate back 
into the 50s, this new pattern favors efficient radiational cooling 
at night. Expect widespread lows below freezing for the remainder 
for the forecast period, with valleys potentially bottoming out in 
the low/mid 20s on Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday nights.
